title: Button, knob, dim on a breadboard
heading: Wire an LED and a knob; the button is on the board

things.label: Breadboard
things.title: Half-size breadboard, 400 points
things.text: Holes in the same column and half (a to e, or f to j) are joined under the plastic, so a lead and a wire in the same short strip are connected. The long rails along the edges are joined end to end.

things.label: 330 ohm resistor
things.title: 330 ohm resistor
things.text: Limits the current through the LED to a few milliamps. Orange, orange, brown, gold bands.

things.label: Red LED
things.title: Red LED
things.text: The longer leg is the plus side (anode); the flat edge is the minus side (cathode). It lights when current flows from plus to minus.

things.label: 10 k knob
things.title: 10 k potentiometer (the knob)
things.text: Three pins: the outer two go across the supply, the middle one is the wiper and gives a voltage between 0 V and 3.3 V as you turn.

steps.title: Put the breadboard beside the LaunchPad
steps.text: Set the half-size breadboard on the right with its numbers running up the page. Letters a to j run across it and numbers 1 to 30 run along it, so every hole has a name like j7. The LaunchPad stays unplugged until the last step.
steps.check: The breadboard sits to the right of the LaunchPad. The LaunchPad has no USB cable in it yet.

steps.title: Ground first: LaunchPad GND to the blue rail
steps.text: Push one end of a black jumper wire into the LaunchPad socket J2 pin 20 (GND) and the other end into the top blue rail. Wiring ground first means a part you plug in later is never live without a return path. A rail is a long strip of holes joined end to end, so any hole on it is ground.
steps.check: Both ends of the black wire show their tag: J2 pin 20 (GND) and the top blue rail.

steps.title: 3.3 V to the red rail
steps.text: A red wire from J1 pin 1 (3V3) to the top red rail. Only the knob uses it in this build.

steps.title: Resistor in first
steps.text: Put the 330 ohm resistor (orange, orange, brown) in holes h3 and h6. Without a resistor in series the LED would draw too much current from the pin. A series resistor is one wired in line with a part to limit the current through it.
steps.check: The resistor lies flat across three holes in row h, with its legs in h3 and h6.

steps.title: The LED, long leg toward the resistor
steps.text: Push the LED legs into f6 and f7. The long leg (plus, anode) goes in f6, the same column as the resistor's right leg. The short leg with the flat edge goes in f7. Backwards, it just stays dark.
steps.check: The long leg is in column 6, in line with the resistor's far leg. Nothing else shares column 7 yet.

steps.title: LED minus to ground
steps.text: A black wire from j7 (the short leg's column) to the ground rail closes the loop on the minus side.

steps.title: Signal wire from J4 pin 40
steps.text: A yellow wire from j3, the resistor's left column, to J4 pin 40 (PB4). The chip drives this pin to light the LED. A GPIO (general-purpose input or output) pin is one the program sets high or low.
steps.check: Yellow wire from breadboard j3 to J4 pin 40 (PB4).

steps.title: The button is already on the board
steps.text: The button is S2, the one on the LaunchPad kit's right edge, so there is nothing to wire for it. The program turns on its pull-up: a resistor inside the chip that holds the pin at 3.3 V until the button pulls it to ground, so the pin never floats.
steps.check: S2 is the button at the right edge of the LaunchPad, beside the headers.

steps.title: Run part 1
steps.text: Plug in USB and run the button program. Each press of S2 toggles the LED.
steps.check: LED changes state each time you press S2.

steps.title: The knob in the breadboard
steps.text: Press the 10 k knob into g23, g24 and g25. It has three pins: the outer two go across the supply and the middle one, the wiper, gives a voltage that follows the turn.
steps.check: The knob stands upright with its three pins side by side in row g.

steps.title: Knob to 3.3 V and ground
steps.text: A red wire from j23 to the red rail and a black wire from j25 to the blue rail put 3.3 V across the knob. 3.3 V, not 5 V: the chip's pins cannot take more than that.
steps.check: Red wire at the knob's left pin, black wire at its right pin.

steps.title: Wiper to J1 pin 2
steps.text: An orange wire from j24 (middle pin) to J1 pin 2 (PA25). That pin is an analog input: an ADC (analog-to-digital converter) turns the voltage on it into a number, 0 at 0 V up to 4095 at 3.3 V.
steps.check: Orange wire from j24 to J1 pin 2 (PA25). Turning the knob changes the number the program prints.

steps.title: Run part 2
steps.text: Run the knob program and watch the number in the serial terminal while you turn the knob from one end to the other.
steps.check: The printed number runs near 0 at one end and near 4095 at the other.

steps.title: Same LED, now dimmed
steps.text: No new wire. The LED is on J4 pin 40 (PB4), a pin a timer can drive. PWM (pulse-width modulation) switches the pin on and off thousands of times a second; the longer it stays on in each cycle, the brighter the LED looks.

steps.title: Knob sets the brightness
steps.text: Run the dim program. It reads the knob (part 2) and uses the number as the PWM duty (the share of each cycle the pin is on). Turn the knob and the LED goes from off to full.
steps.check: Knob to the left: LED off. Knob to the right: LED full. In between it dims smoothly.
